name: Covadonga
summary: A cave in the side of Mount Auseva where the Asturian chronicles set the victory of Pelagius around 722: a battle known only from sources written 160 years later, and a shrine of the Virgin with royal tombs, a chapel rebuilt after the fire of 1777 and a basilica completed in 1901.
overview: Covadonga is a cave shrine in the Picos de Europa of eastern Asturias, where Asturian tradition places the victory of Pelagius over an Umayyad force around 722. The battle is known only from chronicles written some 160 years later; the cave chapel of the Virgin, the tombs attributed to the first Asturian kings and the basilica of 1877 to 1901 are what the place itself preserves.
knownFor: The Battle of Covadonga of about 722, as told in the Asturian chronicles
The Santa Cueva, cave shrine of Our Lady of Covadonga

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Covadonga is a limestone cave in the side of Mount Auseva, above a spring of the river Deva, in a narrow valley of the Picos de Europa about ten kilometres east of Cangas de Onís in Asturias. Christian tradition places here the battle in which Pelagius of Asturias and his followers turned back an Umayyad force around 722, the victory later remembered as the beginning of the Kingdom of Asturias and of the Christian reconquest of Spain.

No source from the eighth century describes that battle; the story first appears in chronicles written at the Asturian court in the 880s. What the valley preserves is a shrine: a cave chapel of the Virgin, whom Asturians call the Santina, a monastery beside it, tombs that tradition assigns to Pelagius and his son-in-law Alfonso I, and a pink stone basilica completed in 1901.

contentSections.title: The valley and the cave
paragraphs: The cave opens in a cliff partway up the valley wall, and water from inside the mountain falls from beneath it into a pool that feeds the Deva. Below the cave the valley narrows to a gorge, and above it the valley closes against the mountain, which is why the chroniclers could describe an army caught between the slopes with no room to deploy. Higher up lie the lakes of Enol and Ercina and the massif of Peña Santa, 2,596 metres high.

The name is old. The Rotensis, the earlier version of the Chronicle of Alfonso III, calls the place coba dominica, the cave of the Lady, and later medieval forms such as covadómnica and covadónnica lead to Covadonga. Some linguists prefer a Celtic origin, cova d'onnica, the cave of the spring, arguing that a dedication to the Virgin would have produced Covadominga in Asturian. If the traditional reading is right, the cave was already dedicated to Mary when the chronicle was written.

contentSections.title: The battle in the chronicles
paragraphs: The Mozarabic Chronicle of 754, the only Christian history written in Spain within living memory of the Muslim conquest, says nothing of Pelagius or Covadonga. The story comes from two works of the Asturian court: the Chronica Albeldensia, finished in 881 and continued to 883, and the Chronicle of Alfonso III, compiled in the 880s. The latter survives in two versions, the plainer Rotensis and the polished ad Sebastianum, which makes Pelagius a sword-bearer of the last Visigothic kings. Both were written some 160 years after the events, for kings who claimed descent from him.

In their account the Berber governor Munuza, based at Gijón, sent Pelagius to Córdoba on an errand and married his sister in his absence. Pelagius fled to the mountains, and the governor of al-Andalus sent an army under Alqama, together with Oppas, a bishop who had gone over to the conquerors, to talk him into surrender. Pelagius answered from the cave that Christ would save Spain from that little mountain. The attackers' stones and arrows turned back on them, 124,000 died in the valley, and 63,000 more were crushed as they fled when a mountainside fell into the river at Cosgaya in Liébana. Oppas was captured, Alqama killed, and Munuza died soon afterwards fighting the Asturians.

These are miracle stories on biblical models, with numbers no army in eighth-century Spain could have fielded. The Arabic record is late and slight. Al-Maqqari, a North African scholar writing around 1630 from older Andalusi histories, tells of a rebel named Pelayo in the land the Arabs called Galicia, whose band dwindled to thirty men living on honey in the clefts of the rocks until the Muslims left them alone, asking what harm thirty wild asses could do.

contentSections.title: What historians accept
paragraphs: Most historians accept that a rising in the Asturian mountains defeated a punitive expedition and that Pelagius led it; they disagree about nearly everything else. Claudio Sánchez-Albornoz dated the battle to 722, under the governor Anbasa, while Julia Montenegro and Arcadio del Castillo argue for 718, under al-Hurr. The Zaragoza medievalist José Luis Corral doubts that the battle took place at all and treats it as an invention of the chroniclers of Alfonso III, while Ignacio Ruiz de la Peña and Luis García Moreno see a real local victory that confirmed Pelagius as leader of an alliance of Visigothic refugees and Asturian nobles.

The historian Pedro Chalmeta noted that parts of the Covadonga story closely resemble the Chronicle of 754's account of a campaign in the Pyrenees, which raises the possibility that the Asturian writers borrowed from it. The succession that followed is better grounded: Pelagius ruled a small realm from Cangas de Onís until his death in 737, his son Favila succeeded him, and his son-in-law Alfonso I, king from 739 to 757, carried Asturian raids south into the Duero valley.

contentSections.title: The royal tombs
paragraphs: Asturian tradition records that Pelagius died at Cangas in 737 and was buried with his wife Gaudiosa in the church of Santa Eulalia at Abamia, where two empty sarcophagi are still shown. The belief that their remains were later moved to Covadonga comes from the sixteenth-century royal chronicler Ambrosio de Morales, who wrote that Alfonso X of Castile ordered the transfer; many historians doubt that it took place.

The cave now holds two tombs, one inscribed for Pelagius, Gaudiosa and a sister of the king, and one for Alfonso I and Pelagius's daughter Ermesinda. The chests and their inscriptions are post-medieval, and they mark where tradition, not archaeology, places the first kings of Asturias.

contentSections.title: The Santa Cueva
paragraphs: Later tradition credits Alfonso I with the first church in the cave, a wooden building with three altars to the Virgin, John the Baptist and Saint Andrew, given to Benedictine monks; no document of his reign confirms it. The monastery of San Pedro below the cave keeps parts of a Romanesque church with three stepped apses, the oldest standing fabric on the site, and the cult of the Virgin of the cave drew pilgrims from across Asturias.

Until 1777 the cave church was built of wood and hung from the rock above the waterfall. That year a fire destroyed it, the wooden lining of the cave and the old image of the Virgin. In 1778 the chapter of Oviedo cathedral gave the shrine a painted wooden Virgin and Child of the sixteenth century, which was kept in the nearby collegiate church until a new chapel was ready in the cave in 1820. The architect Ventura Rodríguez designed a large classical sanctuary to replace the lost church, but it was never built.

The nineteenth-century chapel seen in early photographs was replaced in the twentieth century by the present neo-Romanesque chapel of Luis Menéndez-Pidal, reached by 103 steps from the pool or through a tunnel in the rock. During the Spanish Civil War the image was hidden, taken to Paris and found in the Spanish embassy there in 1939, and it was back in the cave on 6 August that year.

contentSections.title: The basilica and the national shrine
paragraphs: In the nineteenth century Covadonga became a national shrine. In 1857 the dukes of Montpensier raised an obelisk on the meadow below, where tradition says Pelagius was proclaimed king. A new church on the spur facing the cave was the idea of Roberto Frassinelli, a German draughtsman settled at nearby Corao, and with the backing of Alfonso XII work began in 1877 under the architect Federico Aparici, who completed a neo-Romanesque basilica of pink local limestone in 1901. It was declared a minor basilica on 11 September that year.

For the twelfth centenary of the battle in 1918 the image of the Santina was crowned, and on 22 July the mountains around the shrine became the Montaña de Covadonga National Park, the first national park in Spain, enlarged in 1995 as the Picos de Europa National Park. The bronze statue of Pelagius beside the basilica, by Gerardo Zaragoza, dates from 1964.

contentSections.title: Covadonga in memory
paragraphs: The Asturian kings used Covadonga to tie their kingdom to the Visigothic past. The chronicles of the 880s present Pelagius as a Gothic noble restoring the kingdom of Toledo, a claim that justified Alfonso III's expansion to the south. The Cross of Victory, a jewelled cross made for Alfonso III and Queen Jimena in 908 and kept in Oviedo cathedral, was later said to enclose the oak cross Pelagius carried at Covadonga, a tradition its own inscription of 908 does not mention.

Thirteenth-century Castilian historians such as Rodrigo Jiménez de Rada retold and enlarged the story, and in the sixteenth century Ambrosio de Morales made it the opening of Spain's Christian history. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries Covadonga became the symbolic cradle of the Spanish nation, visited by kings and in 1989 by Pope John Paul II, while historians came to see its battle as one local success among many, magnified to give a long and broken process a single starting point.

timeline.title: Battle of Covadonga
timeline.description: According to the Asturian chronicles, Pelagius and his followers defeat an army under Alqama at the cave.

timeline.title: Death of Pelagius
timeline.description: Pelagius dies at Cangas de Onís; tradition later places his tomb in the cave.

timeline.title: Reign of Alfonso I
timeline.description: Later tradition credits Pelagius's son-in-law with the first wooden church in the cave.

timeline.title: A silent chronicle
timeline.description: The Mozarabic Chronicle, written within living memory of the conquest, does not mention Pelagius.

timeline.title: Chronicle of Alfonso III
timeline.description: The fullest miracle story of the battle is compiled, calling the cave coba dominica.

timeline.title: Chronica Albeldensia
timeline.description: The first surviving account of the battle is written at the Asturian court.

timeline.title: Cross of Victory
timeline.description: Alfonso III has the jewelled cross made that later tradition links to Pelagius.

timeline.title: Fire in the cave
timeline.description: The wooden church and the old image of the Virgin are destroyed.

timeline.title: A new Santina
timeline.description: The chapter of Oviedo cathedral gives the shrine a sixteenth-century image of the Virgin.

timeline.title: The obelisk
timeline.description: The dukes of Montpensier mark the traditional place of Pelagius's proclamation.

timeline.title: Basilica begun
timeline.description: Work starts on Federico Aparici's basilica, to a design first proposed by Roberto Frassinelli.

timeline.title: Minor basilica
timeline.description: The completed basilica of Santa María la Real receives its title.

timeline.title: National park
timeline.description: The twelfth centenary brings the first national park in Spain, around the shrine.

timeline.title: The image returns
timeline.description: The Santina, hidden and taken to Paris in the Civil War, is restored to the cave.
